question.before: A particle has v(t) = 12−3t m/s for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8 s. It starts at x = 5 m. Positive velocity is along the positive x-axis. What total distance is travelled during the interval? Choose the closest value.
question.after: For 0 ≤ t ≤ 8 s a particle has v(t)=12−3t m/s and starts at x=5 m. A detector moves along the same axis at x_D(t)=5+2t+0.2t² m. A distance recorder is active only when the particle is ahead of the detector by between 0 and 12 m, inclusive. It records the distance travelled by the particle in the laboratory frame only during those active intervals. The accompanying graph represents the particle velocity. What total distance does the recorder register? Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
The velocity changes sign at t = b/a = 4 s. Integrate |v| on either side of that instant: distance = b²/(2a)+(aT−b)²/(2a) = 48 m. The signed displacement is bT−aT²/2 = 0 m, so final x = 5 m and average speed = 6 m/s.
For the requested outcome — What total distance is travelled during the interval? — the result is 48 m.
explanation.after: The separation is z=x−x_D=10t−1.7t². The condition 0≤z≤12 gives [0,1.67955232] and [4.20280062,5.88235294] s. The particle reverses at 4 s, outside both intervals: its velocity is positive on the first and negative on the second. Integrating |v| over these two intervals gives [x(a)−x(0)]+[x(b)−x(c)]=21.1764706 m. The full-interval triangle area would count inactive motion; twice the 12 m relative-distance window also fails because the detector accelerates.

subtopic.before: Find the heat generated in the third trial over a 2 m descent
subtopic.after: Find the total distance travelled by the table block in the third trial, including the motion after the cut.

question.before: A 4 kg block on a horizontal rough table is connected over a smooth massless pulley to a hanging mass. In one trial a hanging mass 3 kg descends with acceleration 3.142857143 m/s². In another, a hanging mass 2 kg is initially pulled upward and, while still moving upward, has downward acceleration 4.666666667 m/s². The same kinetic friction coefficient applies. An additional hanging mass 5 kg is then used and moves downward from rest. Take g=10 m/s². Find the heat generated in the third trial over a 2 m descent. Choose the closest value.
question.after: A block of unknown mass M slides on a horizontal rough table and is connected by a light string over a smooth massless pulley to a hanging mass. In one trial a 3 kg hanging mass descends with acceleration 2 m/s². In a second trial a 2 kg hanging mass is initially moving upward and, while still moving upward, has downward acceleration 4 m/s². The kinetic friction coefficient is the same in both directions. In a third trial a 5 kg hanging mass descends from rest. After it has descended 2 m, the string is cut without an impulse; the table block then slides freely until it stops. Use g=10 m/s² and assume the third trial starts sliding as stated. Find the total distance travelled by the table block in the third trial, including the motion after the cut. Choose the closest value.

before.C: 8 J

explanation.before:
For downward motion, (m+h1)a1=h1g−μmg. During upward motion, friction reverses, so (m+h2)a2=h2g+μmg. Both give μ=0.2. With h3, a=4.666666667 m/s² and T=h3(g−a)=26.66666667 N. The two-metre descent takes 0.9258200998 s and generates 16 J of heat.
Requested result: 16 J.
explanation.after: Let the kinetic friction force be f. The two moving trials give 30−f=2(M+3) and 20+f=4(M+2), hence M=6 kg and f=12 N, so μ=0.2. The third acceleration is (50−12)/11=38/11 m/s². After 2 m, v²=152/11 m²/s². With the string cut, deceleration is f/M=2 m/s², so the additional distance is 38/11 m. Total distance = 2+38/11 = 60/11 m.

difficulty_reason.before: Infer friction with a direction reversal, distinguish acceleration from velocity, and solve the new coupled system. Assessed outcome: Find the heat generated in the third trial over a 2 m descent.
difficulty_reason.after: Infer both mass and friction using opposite friction signs, then connect the coupled acceleration to the independent stopping stage.

subtopic.before: Find the first positive turning-point coordinate
subtopic.after: Find the total distance travelled before the particle first remains permanently at rest.

question.before: A 3 kg particle starts from rest at x = 0 on a smooth horizontal line. Its only horizontal force is F(x) = 18−ξx N, where x is in metres. The force remains described by this relation throughout the motion. The recorded value of the first positive turning-point coordinate is 18 m. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with this measurement?
question.after: A 3 kg particle is released from rest at x=0 on a rough horizontal line. An external force F(x)=18−2x N acts throughout, with x in metres and positive force toward increasing x. The coefficients of kinetic and static friction are 0.10 and 0.15 respectively; take g=10 m/s². Whenever the particle stops, apply the static-friction condition before deciding whether it moves again. The line is long enough for the motion. Find the total distance travelled before the particle first remains permanently at rest. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the physical relations below with the missing input ξ. Matching the measured the first positive turning-point coordinate gives ξ=2 in the unit assigned to ξ in the question. Substitution checks the observation:
Integrating F gives K = Ax−Bx²/2. This is largest at x = A/B = 9 m, giving vmax = A/√(Bm) = 7.348469228 m/s. The next zero of K is x = 2A/B = 18 m. Motion about x = A/B is SHM with ω = √(B/m); the turning point is reached after half a period, 3.84764949 s.
explanation.after: Kinetic friction has magnitude 3 N and maximum static friction is 4.5 N. On the first outward leg, work is 15x−x², so the nonzero turning point is x=15 m. There |F|=12 N>4.5 N, so it returns. On a leftward leg the total force is 21−2x; zero net work from 15 gives the next stop at x=6 m. There F=6 N>4.5 N, so it moves right. With force 15−2x during that leg, the next stop is x=9 m. Here F=0 and static friction can hold it. Distance =15+9+3=27 m.

question.before: Two reversible heat engines operate in series between reservoirs at 900 K and 400 K, sharing an intermediate reservoir at T. Their efficiencies are equal. The first engine absorbs 900 J per cycle from the hot reservoir; the second receives all the heat rejected by the first. Find the intermediate temperature. Choose the closest value.
question.after: Two reversible engines operate between 900 K and an intermediate reservoir at T, and between T and 300 K. For each composite cycle the first engine absorbs 1200 J. Only 75% of its rejected heat is supplied to the second engine; the other 25% remains in the externally maintained intermediate reservoir. The two engines produce equal work. All the work of the first engine drives a reversible refrigerator that removes heat from the 300 K reservoir and rejects it to the 900 K reservoir. The second engine work is delivered to an external load. Find the net heat gained by the 300 K reservoir per composite cycle, counting both devices connected to it. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Equal Carnot efficiencies imply 1−T/Th = 1−Tc/T, so T² = ThTc and T = 600 K. Each efficiency is 0.3333333333. The first rejects 600 J to the second, whose work is 200 J. The pair has overall efficiency 1−Tc/Th and produces 500 J.
For the requested outcome — Find the intermediate temperature. — the result is 600 K.
explanation.after: The engine works are W₁=1200(1−T/900) and W₂=0.75×1200(T−300)/900. Equality gives T=4500/7 K and W₁=W₂=2400/7 J. The second engine rejects 0.75×1200×300/900=300 J to the cold reservoir. The refrigerator COP is 300/(900−300)=1/2, so it removes 1200/7 J. Net heat gained is 300−1200/7=900/7 J. The diverted intermediate heat is not sent to the second engine.

difficulty_reason.before: Couple the equal-efficiency condition with heat rejected by the first engine; overall efficiency telescopes. Assessed outcome: Find the intermediate temperature.
difficulty_reason.after: Apply the heat split and equal-work constraint, then combine the engine rejection with a refrigerator heat flow of the opposite sign.

subtopic.after: Express the actual engine efficiency as a percentage of the Carnot efficiency between its reservoirs.

question.before: Two reversible heat engines operate in series between reservoirs at 800 K and ξ K, sharing an intermediate reservoir at T. Their efficiencies are equal. The first engine absorbs 1200 J per cycle from the hot reservoir; the second receives all the heat rejected by the first. The recorded value of the intermediate temperature is 400 K. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with this measurement?
question.after: A heat engine absorbs 1500 J per cycle from an 800 K reservoir and rejects heat only to a 300 K reservoir. Part of its work runs a reversible refrigerator between 200 K and 300 K; the remaining 500 J per composite cycle is delivered to a load. The total heat rejected to the 300 K reservoir by the engine and refrigerator together is 1400 J per composite cycle. The engine need not be reversible. Express the actual engine efficiency as a percentage of the Carnot efficiency between its reservoirs. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the physical relations below with the missing input ξ. Matching the measured the intermediate temperature gives ξ=200 in the unit assigned to ξ in the question. Substitution checks the observation:
Equal Carnot efficiencies imply 1−T/Th = 1−Tc/T, so T² = ThTc and T = 400 K. Each efficiency is 0.5. The first rejects 600 J to the second, whose work is 300 J. The pair has overall efficiency 1−Tc/Th and produces 900 J.
explanation.after: For the combined system, heat removed from 200 K is Q_c=1400+500−1500=400 J. The reversible refrigerator COP=200/(300−200)=2, so its work input is 200 J. The engine therefore produces 700 J, giving η=700/1500=7/15. Its Carnot bound is 1−300/800=5/8. The requested percentage is 100(7/15)/(5/8)=224/3 %. This is below 100%, as required.

difficulty_reason.after: Use the whole-system heat balance to determine refrigerator cooling, recover its work and the engine work, then compare efficiencies without assuming a reversible engine.

question.before: An ideal-gas mixture contains 1 mol of a monatomic gas and ξ mol of a rigid diatomic gas at the same temperature. Vibrational modes are frozen. The mixture is heated by 40 K at constant volume. Use R = 8 J/(mol K); composition stays fixed. The recorded value of the supplied heat is 2880 J. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with this measurement?
question.after: A fixed mixture contains unknown positive amounts of a monatomic and a diatomic ideal gas. In a low-temperature constant-volume calibration, a 40 K increase requires 2080 J and diatomic vibration is frozen. In a separate high-temperature constant-volume calibration of the same amounts, a 40 K increase requires 2720 J and one diatomic vibrational mode is fully active. Use C_V=3R/2, 5R/2 and 7R/2 per mole for the monatomic gas, rigid diatomic gas and vibrating diatomic gas respectively, with R=8 J/(mol K). The mixture is then prepared at 300 K and compressed reversibly and adiabatically to half its initial volume. For this final process, diatomic vibration remains frozen throughout. Find the work done on the mixture in this compression. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the physical relations below with the missing input ξ. Matching the measured the supplied heat gives ξ=3 in the unit assigned to ξ in the question. Substitution checks the observation:
Heat capacities add in extensive form: CV = (3a/2+5b/2)R = 72 J/K; CP = CV+(a+b)R = 104 J/K. Therefore γ = 1.444444444, QV = 2880 J. The diatomic energy increase is (5bR/2)ΔT, a fraction 0.8333333333 of the total.
explanation.after: The two total heat capacities are 52 and 68 J/K. Their difference is n_d R=16 J/K, so n_d=2 mol. From 52=(3/2)n_m R+(5/2)n_d R, n_m=1 mol. In the final process nR=24 J/K and γ−1=nR/C_V=6/13. Therefore T_f=300×2^(6/13), and W_on=ΔU=52×300(2^(6/13)−1)=5881.34744 J. The high-temperature heat capacity is used to determine composition, not for the final adiabatic path.

difficulty_reason.after: Extract composition from the change in active degrees of freedom, choose the correct heat capacity for the final regime, then compute adiabatic work.

Increasing tension by a factor 1.5625 makes the string frequency exceed the fork frequency by 20 Hz. Use the change in beats to determine whether the initial string frequency is above or below the fork frequency. Find the final tension. Choose the closest value.
question.after: A sonometer string has length 0.50 m between bridges and linear density 0.001 kg/m. At initial tension T₀ its fundamental makes 4 beats/s with a 100 Hz fork. Multiplying the tension by 1.5625, without changing length or linear density, gives 20 beats/s with the same fork; the sign of the frequency difference is not supplied. Restore T₀, then shorten the vibrating length to 0.40 m. Tension is supplied by a hanging mass through a smooth pulley. Mass is now added until the fundamental makes 5 beats/s with a 150 Hz fork; a further very small addition of mass increases this beat frequency. Use g=10 m/s² and neglect stretching. Find the total mass added after restoring T₀, in grams. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
The beat measurement allows f = fork ± b₁. Testing the tension change using fnew/f = √(Tnew/T) selects f = 96 Hz; it gives the stated final beat difference. Since v = 2Lf = 96 m/s and v² = T/μ, initial tension is 9.216 N, final tension 14.4 N, and the initial second harmonic is 192 Hz.
For the requested outcome — Find the final tension. — the result is 14.4 N. The first observation gives 96 or 104 Hz. The tension multiplier raises these to 120 or 130 Hz; only 120 Hz exceeds the 100 Hz fork by 20 Hz.
explanation.after: Initial candidates are 96 and 104 Hz. Multiplication by √1.5625=1.25 gives 120 or 130 Hz; only 120 gives 20 beats with 100, so f₀=96 Hz and T₀=4L²μf₀²=9.216 N. In the final trial, increasing tension increases beats, so the final string frequency is above 150: f=155 Hz, not 145. At length 0.40 m the required tension is 4×0.40²×0.001×155²=15.376 N. Added mass =(15.376−9.216)/10=0.616 kg=616 g.

question.before: Resistors 2 kΩ and 3 kΩ are in series across an ideal 12 V source. A voltmeter of resistance 6 kΩ is connected across the second resistor. All components are ohmic. Find the power dissipated inside the voltmeter. Choose the closest value.
question.after: In the illustrated divider, the ideal source is 12 V and the voltmeter resistance is 6 kΩ. The fixed positive resistances R1 and R2 are unknown. With the meter across R2 as drawn, it reads 6 V. In a separate measurement it is moved across R1 and reads 4 V; no other load is present in either trial. Remove the meter and connect a load R_L across R2. All resistances are ohmic. Find the smallest R_L for which the loaded output across R2 is at least 90% of its no-load value. Choose the closest value.

correct_answer.before: 6 mW

explanation.before:
The meter shunts the second resistor: Rparallel=2 kΩ. The loaded divider then gives 6 V. Comparing this to the unloaded value VR₂/(R₁+R₂) gives a 16.66666667% reduction. Meter power Vmeter²/Rv is 6 mW.
For the requested outcome — Find the power dissipated inside the voltmeter. — the result is 6 mW.
explanation.after: Use kΩ. The first measurement gives R1=6R2/(6+R2); the second gives R2=2×6R1/(6+R1). The unique positive solution is R1=2 kΩ, R2=3 kΩ. The output has open-circuit voltage 7.2 V and Thevenin resistance 2||3=1.2 kΩ. Its loaded/no-load ratio is R_L/(R_L+1.2). Requiring this to be at least 0.90 gives R_L≥10.8 kΩ.

question.before: Positive ions pass undeflected through crossed uniform fields E = 20000 V/m and B₁ = 0.1 T, with velocity perpendicular to both. They then enter a second region containing only a perpendicular magnetic field B₂ = 0.2 T and describe circles of radius 0.05 m. Neglect gravity and relativistic effects. Find their revolution period in the second region. Choose the closest value.
question.after: An ideal positive nonrelativistic particle passes undeflected through crossed fields E=20000 V/m and B₁=0.10 T, perpendicular to its velocity. In a calibration region with perpendicular B₂=0.20 T it describes a circle of radius 0.050 m. In a separate trial the same selected particle crosses a retarding potential difference of 600 V, then enters a magnetic strip normally at its straight near boundary. The strip field has magnitude 0.40 T perpendicular to the motion plane, and its parallel boundaries are 0.012 m apart. There are no other forces or fields, and the strip is unbounded along its boundaries. Find the time from entry to the first crossing of the far boundary, in ns. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Zero force in the selector requires qE=qvB₁, hence v=200000 m/s. In the second region qvB₂=mv²/r, giving q/m=20000000 C/kg. T=2πr/v=1.570796327 × 10⁻⁶ s. Acceleration from rest uses qΔV=mv²/2, so ΔV=1000 V.
For the requested outcome — Find their revolution period in the second region. — the result is 1.571 × 10⁻⁶ s.
explanation.after: The selector fixes v₀=E/B₁=2×10⁵ m/s. Curvature gives q/m=v₀/(B₂r₀)=2×10⁷ C/kg. After retardation, v²=v₀²−2(q/m)600, giving v=126491.106 m/s. In the strip ω=(q/m)B=8×10⁶ s⁻¹ and radius r=v/ω=0.0158113883 m. Since 0.012<r, the far boundary is reached on the first forward arc. Its normal displacement is r sin(ωt)=0.012, so t=asin(0.012/r)/ω=107.711737 ns.

question.before: A series circuit has inductance ξ H, total resistance 6 Ω and an ideal 18 V DC source. At t=0 the switch closes with zero current. For this transient use I(t)=(V/R)(1−exp(−Rt/L)). Consider the instant when the current is 0.75 times its final value. The recorded value of the elapsed time is 0.6931471806 s. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with this measurement?
question.after: A coil with unknown inductance L and positive resistance r is connected to an ideal 18 V source at t=0 with zero current. The steady current is 3 A, and the current first reaches 1.5 A at time (ln 2)/2 s. At twice that time, a switch instantaneously reverses the source polarity and inserts an extra 6 Ω in series. The coil current is continuous at switching and the circuit remains closed. Inductance is constant. Find the time after switching at which the current first becomes 0.75 A in the direction opposite to its original direction. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the physical relations below with the missing input ξ. Matching the measured the elapsed time gives ξ=3 in the unit assigned to ξ in the question. Substitution checks the observation:
Set I/I∞=0.75 in the supplied exponential relation: t=−(L/R)ln(1−f)=0.6931471806 s. At I=2.25 A, stored energy LI²/2=7.59375 J. Kirchhoff’s law gives L dI/dt=V−IR; multiplying by I gives magnetic-energy growth 10.125 W.
explanation.after: The original steady state gives r=18/3=6 Ω. Half-growth takes (L/r)ln2=(ln2)/2, so L=3 H. At twice that time the initial-direction current is 3(1−1/4)=2.25 A. After switching, total resistance is 12 Ω and the signed steady current is −18/12=−1.5 A. Hence I=−1.5+3.75 exp(−4τ). Setting I=−0.75 gives exp(−4τ)=1/5, so τ=(ln5)/4 s. The zero crossing occurs earlier.

question.after: A coil with unknown positive resistance r and inductance L has reached steady current from an ideal 18 V source. Its stored magnetic energy is 6.75 J. In a calibration decay, the source is removed and an extra 6 Ω resistor completes the closed coil loop; the total charge passing through this resistor over the full decay is 0.375 C. In a fresh identical decay, at the instant current falls to 1 A, the 18 V source is reconnected in the original current direction while the extra 6 Ω remains. explanation.before:
Use the physical relations below with the missing input ξ. Matching the measured the stored magnetic energy gives ξ=6 in the unit assigned to ξ in the question. Substitution checks the observation:
Set I/I∞=0.75 in the supplied exponential relation: t=−(L/R)ln(1−f)=0.6931471806 s. At I=2.25 A, stored energy LI²/2=7.59375 J. Kirchhoff’s law gives L dI/dt=V−IR; multiplying by I gives magnetic-energy growth 10.125 W.

question.before: A conducting rod of length 0.5 m slides at constant speed on smooth horizontal rails in a uniform perpendicular magnetic field 2 T. The closed circuit has total resistance 4 Ω and negligible inductance. A horizontal external force 2 N balances the magnetic drag. Rails and field are long enough for steady motion. Find the Joule-heating power. Choose the closest value.
question.after: A conducting rod of mass 0.50 kg and length 0.50 m slides to the right on horizontal rails as illustrated. The uniform field into the page is 2.0 T; total closed-loop resistance is 4.0 Ω and inductance is negligible. The kinetic friction force on the rod has constant magnitude 0.50 N while it moves. A constant 2.0 N force to the right first maintains steady motion. This applied force is then removed abruptly. The rails and magnetic field extend through the entire subsequent motion; the rod eventually stops. Neglect all other losses. Find the total Joule heat generated after the applied force is removed. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Force balance gives F=BIL, so I=2 A. Motional emf BLv=IR then gives v=8 m/s. Mechanical power Fv equals I²R=16 W. For distance d, charge ∫I dt=BLd/R, giving 0.5 C for 2 m.
For the requested outcome — Find the Joule-heating power. — the result is 16 W.
explanation.after: Magnetic drag is bv with b=(BL)²/R=0.25 N s/m. The initial steady speed is (2−0.5)/0.25=6 m/s. During coasting, m dv/dt=−f−bv. The stopping distance is ∫₀⁶ mv/(f+bv) dv = (m/b)[6−(f/b)ln(1+6b/f)] =12−4ln4 m. Initial kinetic energy is 9 J; friction dissipates 0.5(12−4ln4) J. The rest becomes Joule heat: 9−6+2ln4=3+2ln4 J. All energy has been accounted for when the rod stops.

difficulty_reason.after: Infer steady speed with two drag mechanisms, integrate the coasting dynamics, and separate frictional dissipation from electrical heating.

question.before: A plane sinusoidal electromagnetic wave in vacuum has peak electric-field amplitude 200 V/m and frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. A detector of area ξ cm² is perpendicular to propagation and absorbs 0.6 of the incident energy. Use c=3 × 10⁸ m/s and ε₀=8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m; average intensity is ε₀cE₀²/2. For photon calculations use h=6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The recorded value of the average absorbed power is 0.003186 W. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with this measurement?
question.after: A plane sinusoidal electromagnetic wave in vacuum, of peak electric field 200 V/m, illuminates a flat opaque sheet of unknown actual area A at an unknown oblique angle θ to its normal (0<θ<90°). The sheet absorbs a fraction α of the incident power and reflects the rest specularly; there is no transmission. Measurements give absorbed power 0.0025488 W, time-averaged force normal to the sheet 1.58592×10⁻¹¹ N, and force parallel to the sheet 5.0976×10⁻¹² N in the direction of the incident tangential momentum. Use ε₀=8.85×10⁻¹² F/m and c=3×10⁸ m/s. The beam fully covers the sheet. Find A in cm². Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the physical relations below with the missing input ξ. Matching the measured the average absorbed power gives ξ=1 in the unit assigned to ξ in the question. Substitution checks the observation:
The peak magnetic field is E₀/c=6.666666667 × 10⁻⁷ T. Time-averaging the squared sinusoidal field gives intensity 53.1 W/m². Convert the detector area to m² and multiply by absorptance to get 0.003186 W; in 60 s it absorbs 0.19116 J. Independently, λ=c/f=600 nm. Each photon has energy hf; the absorbed photon rate is Pabsorbed/(hf)=9.610859729 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹.
explanation.after: The average incident intensity is I=ε₀cE₀²/2=53.1 W/m². Let P=IA cosθ be power intercepted by the sheet. Specular reflection transfers no tangential momentum, so F_parallel=αP sinθ/c=P_abs sinθ/c. Thus sinθ=cF_parallel/P_abs=0.6 and cosθ=0.8. Normal force obeys cF_normal=(2−α)P cosθ=(2P−P_abs)cosθ. This gives P=0.004248 W and α=0.6. Therefore A=P/(I cosθ)=10⁻⁴ m²=1 cm². All inferred fractions and angles are physical.

question.before: Two coherent beams have the same frequency and the same fixed linear polarisation. Their interference pattern has maximum intensity ξ W/m² and minimum intensity 9 W/m². Let I₁ be the larger individual-beam intensity and I₂ the smaller. The recorded value of intensity in the original interference pattern where the phase difference is 90° is 29 W/m². Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with this measurement?
question.after: Two coherent beams of the same frequency and fixed linear polarisation produce maximum intensity 49 W/m² and minimum intensity 9 W/m². At a chosen point, the optical path of the stronger beam exceeds that of the weaker by λ/6 modulo λ. A nonreflecting neutral filter is placed in the stronger beam, multiplying its intensity by 1/4 without a phase change. A transparent plate of refractive index 1.5 and thickness λ/2 is also inserted normally in that beam, replacing the same thickness of air. Here λ is the wavelength in air; ignore absorption by the plate. Find the resulting intensity at that point. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the physical relations below with the missing input ξ. Matching the measured intensity in the original interference pattern where the phase difference is 90° gives ξ=49 in the unit assigned to ξ in the question. Substitution checks the observation:
Maximum and minimum amplitudes are √I₁+√I₂ and √I₁−√I₂. Adding and subtracting their measured square roots gives I₁=25, I₂=4 W/m². Quarter intensity means half amplitude, giving a new maximum of 20.25 W/m². At 90° the cross term vanishes and intensity is I₁+I₂=29 W/m².
explanation.after: Let a≥b be the original field-amplitude factors. Then a+b=√49=7 and a−b=√9=3, so a=5, b=2 and individual intensities are 25 and 4. The filter changes the stronger amplitude to 2.5. The plate adds optical path (1.5−1)λ/2=λ/4. Total path excess is λ/6+λ/4=5λ/12 and phase difference is 5π/6. Thus I=2.5²+2²+2×2.5×2 cos(5π/6)=10.25−5√3 W/m².

question.before: A photoelectric apparatus displays stopping reading S=Kmax/e+δ, where δ is an unknown constant instrumental offset. For photon energies ξ and 5 eV the displayed readings are 0.6 and 2.6 V. An independent calibration shows display δ=0.1 V when true voltage is zero. Under illumination with photon energy 4 eV, emitted electrons are accelerated through a further 2 V. Use λ(nm)=√[0.0150/K(eV)] for a nonrelativistic electron and hc=1240 eV nm. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: the final de Broglie wavelength of the fastest electrons = 0.06546536707 nm. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
question.after: A photoelectric apparatus displays S=aV_stop+δ, with unknown positive dimensionless gain a and unknown constant offset δ in volts. For photon energies 3 eV and 5 eV on the same metal, the readings are 0.8 V and 3.2 V respectively. In a separate measurement using 4 eV photons on this metal, the fastest photoelectrons are accelerated through an additional 2 V; their final de Broglie wavelength is √(0.0150/3.5) nm. Use λ(nm)=√[0.0150/K(eV)] for a nonrelativistic electron. The work function, gain and offset stay fixed; there are no contact-potential shifts. Find the offset δ. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=3 in the units assigned in the stem.
Correct the offset before using Einstein’s equation: work function φ=2.5 eV. The second measurement checks the same φ. For E3 the maximum kinetic energy is 1.5 eV; after extra acceleration it is 3.5 eV. The final matter wavelength is 0.06546536707 nm, speed ratio 1.527525232, and optical threshold wavelength 496 nm.
explanation.after: The stopping potential changes by 2 V when photon energy changes by 2 eV, so a=(3.2−0.8)/2=1.2. The final wavelength gives kinetic energy 3.5 eV. Removing the added 2 eV leaves emitted K_max=1.5 eV for 4 eV photons, hence the work function is 2.5 eV. At 3 eV illumination the true stopping potential is 0.5 V. Consequently δ=0.8−1.2×0.5=0.2 V. The second reading verifies 1.2×2.5+0.2=3.2 V.

question.before: An ideal diode has its anode at node X and cathode at a fixed +3 V reference. Node X connects to a +12 V ideal source through 300 Ω and to ground through 600 Ω. An ideal conducting diode has zero drop; a reverse-biased diode carries no current. The reference can absorb current. As the positive supply voltage is reduced, at what supply value does the diode just cease to conduct? Choose the closest value.
question.after: Use the illustrated ideal-diode network: node X is fed through 300 Ω and connected to ground through 600 Ω; the diode anode is at X and its cathode at a fixed +3 V reference that can absorb current. The source labelled +12 V in the diagram is now varied periodically: it rises linearly from 0 to 12 V in 0.5 s, then falls linearly to 0 in the next 0.5 s. The ideal diode has zero forward drop and no reverse current. There is no capacitance or inductance, so the circuit is in its DC state at each instant. Find the heat generated in the 300 Ω resistor during one complete cycle, in mJ. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
With the diode open, the divider would give 8 V, above the reference, so the diode conducts and X is clamped. Kirchhoff’s law gives diode current 0.025 A. Load power is Vclamp²/Rl=0.015 W. At the boundary, open-circuit divider voltage equals Vclamp, requiring supply 4.5 V.
For the requested outcome — As the positive supply voltage is reduced, at what supply value does the diode just cease to conduct? — the result is 4.5 V.
explanation.after: With the diode off, V_X=2V_s/3, so conduction begins at V_s=4.5 V. Below this threshold the 300 Ω voltage is V_s/3; above it V_X=3 V and the resistor voltage is V_s−3. The triangular cycle spends equal time per voltage interval, with total dt=dV_s/12 for both ramps together. Hence Q=(1/3600)[∫₀^4.5(V_s/3)² dV_s+∫₄.₅^12(V_s−3)² dV_s] = (3.375+241.875)/3600 J=0.068125 J=68.125 mJ.

subtopic.before: If zero correction is omitted, find the signed percentage bias in inferred density relative to the corrected value
subtopic.after: Find the largest density in g/cm³ consistent with these bounds, using the exact cylinder-volume formula rather than a first-order percentage approximation.

question.before: A vernier has 20 divisions equal to 19 main-scale divisions; one main-scale division is 1 mm. With jaws closed its zero lies to the right and division 3 coincides. For a solid sphere the main-scale reading is ξ mm and division 3 coincides. The sphere’s mass is 7.23456 g. The displacement of water measured independently is 0.90432 cm³. Use π=3.14. Treat the mass and displacement measurement as exact; the corrected diameter has maximum uncertainty one least count. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: If zero correction is omitted, the signed percentage bias in inferred density relative to the corrected value = -3.658167134 %. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
question.after: A vernier has 20 divisions equal to 19 main-scale divisions, and one main-scale division is 1 mm. For a solid cylinder, the indicated diameter has main-scale reading 10 mm and coincidence 5; the indicated height has main-scale reading 20 mm and coincidence 7. In a separate closed-jaw calibration the indicated positive zero error is 0.15 mm. Treat each of these three indicated readings as having an independent maximum error of half a least count. The same unknown actual zero error applies to both cylinder readings. The cylinder mass is (16.01±0.01) g. All values within these error bounds are admissible; use π=3.141592654 and ignore deformation. Find the largest density in g/cm³ consistent with these bounds, using the exact cylinder-volume formula rather than a first-order percentage approximation. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=12 in the units assigned in the stem.
Least count is 1−19/20=0.05 mm. Subtract the positive zero error, giving d=12 mm and V=0.90432 cm³, consistent with the stated displacement. Density is 8 g/cm³. Since ρ∝d⁻³, its first-order percentage bound is 1.25% and absolute bound 0.1 g/cm³. Without correction the larger diameter lowers inferred density; signed bias=-3.658167134%.
explanation.after: The least count is 1−19/20=0.05 mm, so each indicated-reading error is bounded by 0.025 mm. Diameter indication is 10.25 mm and height indication is 20.35 mm. To maximize density, take mass 16.02 g, both indications at their lower bounds, and the common actual zero error at its upper bound 0.175 mm. These choices are simultaneously allowed. Thus d_min=10.05 mm and h_min=20.15 mm. The density maximum is 16.02/[π(10.05)²(20.15)/(4×1000)]=10.0222552 g/cm³. The common zero error is not an independent correction for each dimension.

question.before: A wire in the left gap of an ideal metre bridge balances against 4 Ω in the right gap at ξ cm from the left. Its length is 3 m. A screw gauge of pitch 0.5 mm with 50 divisions shows main-scale reading 0.5 mm and circular reading 32; its positive zero error is 2 divisions. Neglect bridge end corrections. Take π=3.14. In a separate trial, the same wire carries 0.5 A for 60 s with unchanged resistance. The recorded value of heat generated in the wire during the separate current trial is 90 J. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with this measurement?
question.after: A uniform metre-bridge wire has an unknown resistance per unit length. Its left end connection has resistance r_a and its right end connection has resistance r_b=0.003 Ω; both lie in series with the corresponding wire segments, while gap connections are ideal. An unknown resistor X in the left gap and a 4 Ω standard in the right gap balance at 61 cm from the left end of the uniform wire. After interchanging only the gap resistors, balance is at 40 cm from the same left end. Separately, X generates 90 J of heat while carrying 0.50 A for 60 s at unchanged resistance. The bridge wire diameter is measured with a screw gauge of pitch 0.5 mm and 50 circular divisions: main-scale reading 0.5 mm, circular reading 32, and positive zero error 2 divisions. Take π=3.14. Find the resistivity of the uniform bridge wire, in units of 10⁻⁸ Ω m. Choose the closest value.

explanation.before:
Use the physical relations below with the missing input ξ. Matching the measured heat generated in the wire during the separate current trial gives ξ=60 in the unit assigned to ξ in the question. Substitution checks the observation:
The gauge least count is 0.01 mm; subtract its positive zero error to get diameter 0.8 mm. The bridge gives X=Rl/(100−l) =6 Ω. Then ρ=Xπd²/(4L)=1.0048 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Ignoring the zero error changes the squared diameter and overestimates ρ by 5.0625%. Swapping gaps replaces l by 100−l=40 cm. With resistance X found from the bridge, the separate trial produces I²Xt=90 J.
explanation.after: The heating trial gives X=90/(0.50²×60)=6 Ω. Let q be wire resistance per cm, and a=r_a/q, b=r_b/q be equivalent end lengths in cm. The two balances give (61+a)/(39+b)=6/4 and (40+a)/(60+b)=4/6. Solving gives a=2 cm and b=3 cm; therefore q=0.003/3=0.001 Ω/cm=0.1 Ω/m. Gauge least count is 0.01 mm, and corrected diameter is 0.5+(32−2)0.01=0.80 mm. Hence ρ=(resistance/length)×area=0.1×3.14×(0.0008)²/4=5.024×10⁻⁸ Ω m.
